items.title: Embodied AI Lab for Education
items.text:
Welcome to the Embodied AI Lab for Education, an open-source platform providing practical guides, software, and teaching resources for robotics and embodied intelligence.

The lab supports research-driven education through hands-on experiments in perception, localization, control, and autonomous systems. Its facilities include Unitree Go2 quadruped robots, a Qualisys motion-capture system, Crazyflie 2.1+ drones, an ultra-wideband (UWB) localization network, wooden stairs and stands, and custom-designed handheld platforms.

This documentation introduces the main hardware platforms and experimental tools available in the lab. You will learn how to work with:

  • Qualisys camera-based motion tracking
  • Crazyflie 2.1+ drones
  • Ultra-wideband localization
  • Visual-inertial odometry
  • LiDAR-inertial odometry
  • Manus motion-capture gloves

Together, these tools form a flexible platform for developing, testing, and demonstrating embodied AI methods.

The following section, Unitree Go2 Sim-to-Real, provides a complete workflow for training locomotion policies in simulation, validating them across simulators, and deploying them on a real Unitree Go2 robot.

items.title: Real-world Setup
items.text: We mount a Jetson Orin AGX 64GB on the Unitree Go2 robot. For detailed hardware information and CAD files, please refer to REASAN.

items.title: Flash the System
items.text:
• Hardware setup follow the guidance
    • First finish L4T BSP flash step
  • SDK Manager Step1
    • choose Jetson AGX Orin [64GB developer kit version], JetPack 6.2.1
    • Do NOT select Host Machine
  • SDK Manager Step2
    • Only select the first Jetson Linux
    • Do NOT select Jetson Runtime Components Click Contine Click Create Then click Continue and input your sudo password
  • SDK Manager Step3 IMPORTANT! Choose RUNTIME and NVME (if with ssd inside) Click Flash After a while, it goes back to this page again Usually this step takes about 5-8 minutes
  • SDK Manager Step4 Done!

items.title: Install SDK Components
items.text:
First make sure you finish first flashing step and install ubuntu already, finish ubuntu initial setups first. Do NOT run sudo apt update or upgrade at this step, it may cause version mismatch errors later. Follow this guide.

  • SDK Manager Step 1 No need to make AGX Orin be in Force Recovery Mode, just wait for some time then it can be detected.
  • SDK Manager Step 2 Select SDK components we want: When you click SDK components, some Runtime components required for SDK components will be automatically selected. Click Continue and input your sudo password.
  • SDK Manager Step 3 And set configuration like this. Input username and password you set for ubuntu in jetson agx orin: Click install: Notes: Sometimes it encounters device image version matching requirement, follow this guide. This may be caused by sudo apt update and upgrade at initial setups of ubuntu, you can reflash Jetson AGX Orin to solve this mismatch.
  • SDK Manager Step 4

items.title: IsaacLab
items.text: Code is available here.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
First create a new conda environment: 

conda create -n env_go2 python=3.10
conda activate env_go2

Install PyTorch: 

pip install torch==2.7.0 torchvision==0.22.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

Install IsaacSim 4.5.0: 

pip install --upgrade pip
pip install 'isaacsim[all,extscache]==4.5.0' --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com

Install IsaacLab and others inside the cloned folder: 

./isaaclab.sh --install
pip install -e ./rsl_rl
pip install -e ./asig_sim2real

items.title: Training and Playing
items.text:
python scripts/train.py --run_name policy_1

Training output would be something like this: 

python scripts/play.py --load_run policy_1

For the first time, it may take some time to build the shaders.

items.title: Export ONNX Model
items.text:
After being played, the ONNX model of the policy will be exported, which is needed for deployment.

Inside logs/rsl_rl/asig_sim2real/policy_1/exported you can find the policy.onnx exported just now. Copy this file to the deployment folder:

cp ./logs/rsl_rl/asig_sim2real/policy_1/exported/policy.onnx ./deployment/model

items.title: Build deployment code
items.text:
Now we have the ONNX model, we can build the deployment code.

First install dependencies:

  • Install ROS2 Humble following this guide

  • Install unitree_sdk2

  • Install other dependencies 

    sudo apt install libeigen3-dev libfmt-dev

  • Install onnxruntime

    • Go to the release page and download prebuilt binaries. Please download this file (tested): onnxruntime-linux-x64-gpu-1.22.0.tgz

    • Extract the folder and copy the “include” folder to “/usr/local”.

    • Copy the “lib” folder as “/usr/local/lib64”.

    • Copy the “lib/cmake” folder to “/usr/local/lib”.

    • Add “/usr/local/lib64” to your “LD_LIBRARY_PATH”: 

      export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

  • Download TensorRT 10.9 GA from here and extract to a separate folder. You should download this one: TensorRT 10.9 GA for Linux x86_64 and CUDA 12.0 to 12.8 TAR Package. Then Add “lib” folder of extracted TensorRT to your “LD_LIBRARY_PATH”: 

    export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/absolute/path/to/tensorrt/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

  • Install cuda-12.8 and cudnn-9 and add to LD_LIBRARY_PATH Install cuda-12.8 follow this. Install cudnn-9 follow this. Then: 

    export PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.8/bin${PATH:+:${PATH}}
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.8/lib64${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH}}

Now the dependencies should be fine, go back to the asig_sim2real folder and build the deployment code: 

cd deployment
./run_build.sh

items.title: Deploy in MuJoCo.
items.text:
Follow this link to install unitree_mujoco to a separate folder. If you install c++ version, follow official guidance to install mujoco.

Make sure you install MuJoCo 3.2.7 using: 

pip install mujoco==3.2.7

Notes: You need to clone unitree_mujoco to local After installation following official guidance, open unitree_mujoco/simulate_python/config.py, set USE_JOYSTICK = 0. In MuJoCo it should look like this:

After installation, launch the unitree_mujoco simulator (both Python and C++ version work) in unitree_mujoco folder 

# this is for c++ version
cd unitree_mujoco/simulate/build
./unitree_mujoco # assuming you have build output here

# this is for python version
cd unitree_mujoco/simulate_python
python3 ./unitree_mujoco.py

Finally, start the control nodes in asig_sim2real/deployment folder (If you encounter errors, try to deactivate the conda environment): 

# terminal 1: deploy onnx model
./locomotion_node --net lo --policy loco_policy # or loco_policy (the pretrained policy)
# terminal 2: keyboard control
python terminal_control.py

items.title: Flash Jetson Orin AGX
items.text: First we need to flash Nvidia Jetson Orin AGX and install SDK packages like cuda, cudnn, tensorrt and so on. Check the deployment docuement for details on flashing the system and installing components.

items.title: Install Dependencies
items.text:
Log into Jetson AGX Orin ubuntu system and check whether required packages are installed correctly: 

nvcc –version
ls -l /usr/local/cuda
ls /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libcudnn*
ls /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libnvinfer*
If not, you can try to follow the components installation guide again.

Install ROS2 humble.

Install unitree sdk2.

Install unitree sdk2 python follow their official guide. When following the last code block of FAQ-1, change the commands to: 

#use the following commands instead of those given in repository
cd ~/unitree_sdk2_python
export CYCLONEDDS_HOME=/home/usrname/cyclonedds/install
# if this doesn't work, try this one
export CYCLONEDDS_HOME=$HOME/cyclonedds/install

pip3 install -e . --no-build-isolation

Install required packages for the deployment code: 

sudo apt install libeigen3-dev libfmt-dev

Install onnxruntime, compile procedures are based on official manuscript.

  • Onnxruntime v1.23.2: install from source 
    git clone --recursive https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime

sudo apt install -y --no-install-recommends \
build-essential software-properties-common libopenblas-dev \
libpython3.10-dev python3-pip python3-dev python3-setuptools python3-wheel
  • Install cmake 3.28.5, find files in https://cmake.org/files/v3.28/. Choose cmake-3.28.5-linux-aarch64.sh. 
    chmod +x ./cmake-3.28.5-linux-aarch64.sh
sudo ./cmake-3.28.5-linux-aarch64.sh --prefix=/usr/local

# check cmake version; should be 3.28 now
cmake --version

# if you encounter errors or version not update, reboot may simply solve problem
  • Go to cloned onnxruntime project. Make sure you set onnxruntime_BUILD_UNIT_TESTS=OFF , more details in github. 
    ./build.sh --config Release --update --build --parallel --use_tensorrt --cuda_home /usr/local/cuda --cudnn_home /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu --tensorrt_home /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu --skip_tests --cmake_extra_defines 'CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native''onnxruntime_BUILD_UNIT_TESTS=OFF' --build_shared_lib

cd build/Linux/Release
sudo make install

cd /usr/local/lib/cmake/onnxruntime
sudo vim ./onnxruntimeTargets-release.cmake
# change all "lib64" to "lib" and save

items.title: Build Deployment Code
items.text:
# before run this, make sure you source livox_driver, mocap and unitree driver first

cd ~/asig_sim2real/deployment
./run_build.sh

# if you encounter onnxruntime error again, run this:
sudo cp -r /usr/local/include/onnxruntime /usr/local/include/

items.title: Deploy and Control
items.text:
Make sure your Jetson is in the same subnet as your PC. For example, Jetson IP can be 192.168.20.1, and the IP of your PC can be 192.168.20.2. On both computers, set the network IPv4 to be manual, and the network mask should be 255.255.255.0. After this, you should be able to communicate with ROS2 on both computers. Then, similarly to the Sim-to-Sim deployment, run the control script on your PC, and run the deployment code on Jetson: 

# on your pc
python terminal_control.py

# on jetson
export NET_INTERFACE=network # network interface name on jetson connecting to the robot (e.g., eno1)
./locomotion_node --net <network interface> --policy loco_policy # or loco_policy

items.title: DISCLAIMER
items.text:
WARNING — REAL ROBOT DEPLOYMENT

Always validate your controller in MuJoCo simulation before deploying to hardware. This document is provided as-is, for reference only, with no guarantee of correctness or safety.

Real robots can move suddenly and with significant force. Hardware and software setups vary, and behavior that works in simulation may fail on hardware. Before running anything:

  • Keep an emergency stop within reach at all times
  • Clear the workspace of people and obstacles
  • Start with reduced torque/velocity limits
  • Never assume the robot will behave as expected

You are solely responsible for ensuring the safety of people and equipment when using this document and the accompanying code.

items.title: MuJoCo Playground
items.text:
This instruction explains how to train a Unitree Go2 quadruped to track commanded velocities using Reinforcement Learning (RL) in MuJoCo Playground. To follow the steps, refer to our customized open-source repository.

Task: Track body-frame planar velocity commands: \(\mathbf{c} = [v_x^c, v_y^c, \omega_z^c]\) where \(v_x\) and \(v_y\) are the commanded linear velocities in the robot’s body frame, and \(\omega_z\) is the commanded yaw rate. RL algorithm: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)

This instruction uses the Go2JoystickFlatTerrain environment and the RSL-RL implementation of PPO through the learning/train_rsl_rl.py training script.

Note

All parameter values and configuration details presented in this document are set for the current environment and training setup. They should not be interpreted as generic defaults for Unitree Go2 locomotion tasks.

items.title: Observation Space
items.text:
Actor Observation: The actor receives proprioception information, each frame contains 45-dimensional observation:

Term Dimension Noise amplitude Local angular velocity 3 +/-0.2 Projected gravity 3 +/-0.05 Velocity commands 3 None Joint position bias 12 +/-0.01 Joint velocity 12 +/-0.01 Previous actions 12 None

Noise is uniform and independently sampled for each new frame. Actor input: Observation history of concatenating 10 frames (450-dimensional). It supplies short-term temporal context to the feed-forward actor.

Critic Observation: The critic receives the uncorrupted current actor frame and privileged information:

Term Dimension Current actor observation 45 Local linear velocity 3 Base height above ground 1

Critic input: 49-dimensional and contains no history.

items.title: Action Space
items.text:
The policy action is a normalized 12-dimensional vector, one value per actuated Go2 joint in MuJoCo model order: \(\mathbf{a}_t \in [-1, 1]^{12}\). After rollout perturbation noise and clipping, the environment computes:

\[ \mathbf{q}_{target} = \mathbf{q}_{default} + 0.5\mathbf{a}_t \]

where 0.5 is action scale. Note: The action is not a torque command. It is converted to a joint-position target, and the MuJoCo position actuators apply the configured PD gains. See the MuJoCo actuator documentation for the underlying actuation model.

items.title: Rewards
items.text:
At each control step, the environment computes

\[ r_t = \Delta t \sum_i s_i r_i, \qquad \Delta t = 0.02. \]

where \(r_i\) and \(s_i\) represent each reward term and its scale, \(\Delta t\) is the control step. The full rewards, reward scales and definitions are listed below:

Term Scale Definition tracking_lin_vel +1.0 \(\exp\left(-\lVert \mathbf{v}_{xy}^{c}-\mathbf{v}_{xy}^{b}\rVert_2^2/0.25\right)\) tracking_ang_vel +1.0 \(\exp\left(-\left(\omega_z^{c}-\omega_z^{b}\right)^2/0.25\right)\) height +1.0 \(\exp\left(-10 \cdot \left(z_b-0.35\right)^2\right)\) lin_vel_z -1.5 \(\left(v_z^b\right)^2\) action_rate -0.05 \(\lVert \mathbf{a}_t-\mathbf{a}_{t-1}\rVert_2^2\) action -0.1 \(\lVert \mathbf{a}_t\rVert_2^2\) ang_vel_xy -0.05 \(\lVert \boldsymbol{\omega}_{xy}^{b}\rVert_2^2\) orientation -5.0 \(\lVert \mathbf{g}_{xy}^{b}\rVert_2^2\), \(\mathbf{g}^{b}\) is body-frame projected gravity pose +1.2 \(\exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{12}w_j\left(q_j-q_j^{\mathrm{default}}\right)^2\right), \mathbf{w}=[1,1,0.1]^{\times 4}\) stand_still -1.0 \(\mathbb{1}_{\lVert\mathbf{c}\rVert_2<0.01}\sum_{j=1}^{12}\left\|q_j-q_j^{\mathrm{default}}\right\|\) energy -0.001 \(\sum_{j=1}^{12}\left \| \dot{q}_j\right\| \cdot \left\|\tau_j\right\|\)

items.title: Domain Randomization
items.text:
Domain randomization is used to reduce overfitting, improve robustness, and prepare the controller for deployment conditions.

Quantity Distribution Geometry friction scale U(0.5, 2.0) Body mass and inertia scale U(0.85, 1.15) Proportional gain Kp U(25.0, 45.0) Derivative gain Kd U(0.3, 1.6) COM offset x/y +/-0.05 m, z +/-0.04 m External Push U(-1.0, 1.0)

items.title: Environment Configuration
items.text: Parameter Value Physics step, sim_dt 0.004 s (250 Hz) Control step, ctrl_dt 0.02 s (50 Hz) Physics substeps per action 5 Nominal episode length 5,000 control steps (100 s) Sampled time limit 3,750 - 6,250 steps (75 - 125 s) Nominal PD gains Kp = 35.0, Kd = 0.5 Soft joint-limit factor 0.95

items.title: PPO Configuration
items.text: Parameter Value Parallel environments 2,048 Steps per environment and iteration 24 Samples per iteration 49,152 Actor hidden dimensions [512, 256, 128] Critic hidden dimensions [512, 256, 128] Initial Gaussian action standard deviation 0.5 PPO clip parameter 0.2 Discount factor gamma 0.99 GAE parameter lambda 0.95 Learning rate 1e-3 Learning-rate schedule adaptive; target KL 0.01 Learning epochs per iteration 10 Mini-batches per epoch 4 Samples per mini-batch 12,288 Value-loss coefficient 1.0 Entropy coefficient 0.01 Maximum gradient norm 1.0

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Install our customized open-sourced repository and required dependencies. Here we create a conda virtual environment for this task. 

conda create -n env_mujocoplayground python=3.12 -y  
conda activate env_mujocoplayground # make sure environment is always activated in following commands
cd leg-mujoco
pip install -e . # install Go2 customized MuJoCo Playground
# install required dependencies
pip install rsl-rl-lib wandb

items.title: Train the policy
items.text: train-rsl-ppo --env_name=Go2JoystickFlatTerrain

items.title: Play the policy
items.text:
It is necessary to speficy play-only, load_run_name, and checkpoint_num (optional). 

train-rsl-ppo \
  --env_name=Go2JoystickFlatTerrain \
  --play_only \
  --load_run_name=<run_name> \
  --checkpoint_num=<number>
If checkpoint_num is not specified, the latest checkpoint is automatically chosen.

items.title: Export policy in ONNX format
items.text:
This is for Sim-to-Sim validation and real-world deployment, we use ONNX format to deploy. 

train-rsl-ppo \
  --env_name=Go2JoystickFlatTerrain \
  --export_onnx_only \
  --load_run_name=<run_name> \
  --checkpoint_num=<number>

items.title: Sim-to-Sim Validation
items.text: Please refer to Isaaclab Training Sim-to-Sim Deployment with MuJoCo section for details.

items.title: Real-world Deployment
items.text:
The ROS 2/Unitree deployment code lives in deploy and runs exported ONNX policies for Go2JoystickFlatTerrain. See deploy/README.md for setup, configuration, sim-to-sim, and real-robot notes.

  1. Export Policy into ONNX format file and move to deploy/model/.
  2. Check and revise config.yaml. In real robot deployment, some parameters (e.g. Kp and Kd) need to be adjusted based on different robot. Set the correct exported policy path: 
    policy:
  path: "model/policy_deploy.onnx"  # match your own file name
    For the real robot, enable unitree_services: 
    unitree_services:
  enable: true
    Note: This makes the node call Unitree SportClient::StandDown() and MotionSwitcherClient::ReleaseMode() before low-level control. For MuJoCo sim-to-sim validation, set unitree_services to be false. The ROS2 node expects: 
    input:  obs      [1, 450]
output: actions  [1, 12]
    During policy control, the ROS2 node publishes two 12-joint messages in Unitree SDK motor order (FR, FL, RR, RL, with hip/thigh/calf for each leg): 
    - /network_output_raw: unscaled policy actions after finite-value handling and the configured `action_clip`.
- /target_action: final joint-angle commands, computed as `default_angles + network_output_raw * action_scale`.
  3. Build the workspace. Source the ROS 2 and Unitree SDK environment first, then: 
    cd deploy
./run_build.sh
source install/share/go2_joystick_deploy/local_setup.bash
    Note: Source install/share/go2_joystick_deploy/local_setup.bash in every terminal that uses ROS CLI tools with the custom JointAngularPositions message.
  4. Run With Unitree MuJoCo 
    cd deploy
./locomotion_node --net lo --config config.yaml
    In another terminal, run the existing command publisher: 
    python ../deploy/terminal_cmd.py  # or wireless_cmd.py to use joystick controller
  5. Real Robot Notes Hardware setup details depend on the onboard computer, network interface, Unitree SDK installation, and robot safety procedure; for a fuller hardware reference, see REASAN. On shutdown or Ctrl+C, the node interpolates to sit_angles and then sends a damping command.

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
Welcome to the Unitree Go2 Sim-to-Real guide. This documentation walks you through the complete workflow—from policy training in simulation to Sim-to-Sim validation and deployment on a real robot.

The MuJoCo Playground and IsaacLab sections follow the same overall pipeline:

  • Train a PPO policy in simulation
  • Validate it through sim-to-sim transfer
  • Deploy it on the Unitree Go2

The main difference is the simulation platform used for training. The Real-World Setup section covers the required robot hardware, onboard computing configuration, and instructions for flashing the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.

Follow the sections in order to build, validate, and deploy your own Sim-to-Real locomotion pipeline.

items.title: Qualisys Camera Tracking
items.text:
Refer to Qualisys Motion Capture system

Install Qualisys Track Manager on Windows system Install Qualisys ROS2 driver on Linux system

items.title: Get started with Qualisys Track Manager
items.text:
1. Open an existing project by locating to the corresponding folder.
  2. Start by clicking on new. A blank page will appear. Make sure no markers are now in the coverage of qualisys, and then click on Auto-Mask to remove noise. Click on 3D, place the cap on the ground and check if it can be found in 3D view.

items.title: Launching Qualisys ROS2 driver and collect data
items.text:
1. Clone and build the driver
  2. Set host_name in file mocap_ws/src/mocap4ros2_qualisys/qualisys_driver/config/qualisys_driver_params.yaml to the local WiFi IP address
  3. Connect to the local WiFi
  4. Commands to launch node and record data: 
    ros2 launch qualisys_driver qualisys.launch.py 
ros2 run rviz2 rviz2 # visualization if message `tf` is available. Add `tf` to the displays and change the basic frame to world. Names of objects will be shown besides the coordinates
ros2 bag record -o /path/and/bag/name /rigid_bodies /markers

items.title: Install the Crazyflie Client (cfclient)
items.text:
More details can be found here.

  1. Install dependencies 
    sudo apt install git python3-pip libxcb-xinerama0 libxcb-cursor0
# Activate virtual environment to avoid conflicts of dependencies. Here we use Miniconda as an example. 
conda create -n env_1_cfclient python=3.12 # “env_1_cfclient” is the name of this virtual environment and can be changed to other names.
conda activate env_1_cfclient 
pip3 install --upgrade pip
conda deactivate # This command can be skipped if you keep the following steps within the same terminal.

  2. Set USB permissions, see also here for more details. 

    sudo groupadd plugdev
sudo usermod -a -G plugdev $USER
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-bitcraze.rules > /dev/null
# Crazyradio (normal operation)
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTRS{idVendor}=="1915", ATTRS{idProduct}=="7777", MODE="0664", GROUP="plugdev"
# Bootloader
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTRS{idVendor}=="1915", ATTRS{idProduct}=="0101", MODE="0664", GROUP="plugdev"
# Crazyflie (over USB)
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTRS{idVendor}=="0483", ATTRS{idProduct}=="5740", MODE="0664", GROUP="plugdev"
EOF
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
sudo udevadm trigger

  3. Install cfclient 

    conda activate env_1_cfclient # Skip this command if you are already in the virtual environment 
pip3 install cfclient

  4. Launch cfclient 

    conda activate env_1_cfclient # Skip this command if you are already in the virtual environment  
cfclient

items.title: Configure Crazyflie’s address in cfclient for the first use of Crazyflie
items.text:
1. Connect the Crazyflie with computer via micro USB cable
  2. Open cfclient. The interface looks as follows
  3. Click on Scan -> usb://0 will show in the drop down menu -> Click on Connect
  4. After successful connection, define the address by going to tab Connect/Configure 2.x -> In the following window, change the last two digits of Radio Address to e.g., 01 -> Click on Write
  5. Exit cfclient

items.title: Connect to the Crazyflie through Crazyradio
items.text:
The following order matters

  1. Turn on the Crazyflie by connecting it to its battery. A successful start should have LEDs as shown here in Section Getting to know your Crazyflie.
  2. Plug in the Crazyradio
  3. Launch cfclient
  4. Change the following Address to the desired one (e.g., the one just configured before)
  5. Click on Scan to detect available Crazyflie addresses
  6. Select the desired Crazyflie address from the drop down menu
  7. Important: Before clicking on ‘connect’, briefly unplug and then plug in the Crazyradio again
  8. Click on Connect in the cfclient. A successful connection will be shown on the top of the window Connected on radio… Failed connection: always Connecting … Note: This unplug and plug-in action in step 7 helps resolve potential connection issues as noted here, which causes cfclient to get stuck during the connection stage. Although an alternative solution (downgrading the firmware) is mentioned on the same page, it has not been tested yet. If the connection succeeds, the flight data on the right side of cfclient should show the orientation of the Crazyflie. The LEDs on Crazyradio and Crazyflie should look like this: Crazyradio has green & yellow LED on Crazyflie: M1 blinking red twice every second (constantly red means error), M2 & M3 constantly blue, M4 constantly yellow. Other cases please refer to here in section Understanding LEDs.
  9. Optional: Check the box View/Tabs/Parameters to check the available topics.

items.title: Define Crazyflie coordinate in Qualisys
items.text:
1. Attach markers. The arrangement of markers is crucial for accurate pose estimation and precise control of the Crazyflie. Consider using an asymmetric layout of markers. Refer to the example picture below.
  2. Open QTM and define a rigid body for the Crazyflie with the origin set at its center. Make sure that the x-axis is oriented towards the front (as shown in Section Getting to Know Your Crazyflie), and the z-axis points upwards.
  3. Name the rigid body cfx, where x corresponds to the last digits of the Crazyflie's address (as a rule of thumb). For example, if the address is 0xE7E7E7E702, name it cf2; if the address is 0xE7E7E7E701, name it cf1, and so on. This will later be used in the config file.

items.title: Clone the repository and compile
items.text:
mkdir cffly_ws && cd cffly_ws
mkdir src && cd src
git clone https://github.com/IMRCLab/crazyswarm2.git
cd ..
colcon build --symlink-install
source install/setup.bash

To test whether everything has been set up properly: 1. Connect the computer to the Qualysis WiFi 2. Setup config files properly: Change the yaml file crazyswarm2/config/crazyflies.yaml: enable related Crazyflie, make sure its name (cfx) and uri match the names defined in QTM and the address in the cfclient, respectively. Set the hostname in file crazyswarm2/crazyswarm2/crazyflie/config/motion_capture.yaml according to the IP address of Qualisys. 3. Turn on Crazyflie and connect to it through Crazyradio 4. Test whether the Crazyflie can be detected/connected and Qualysis is working well: 

ros2 launch crazyflie launch.py backend:=cflib

Note: For safety reasons of Crazyflie, make sure every following thing looks correct:

  • Check if the Crazyflie's position displayed in the Rviz window reflects its real-world position. If no position is displayed or the position is drifting, something is wrong.
  • Crazyradio & Crazyflie should have LEDs illuminated before.

items.title: Launch an example of Crazyflie taking off & landing using ROS2
items.text:
1. Make sure your computer is connected with Crazyflie through Crazyradio
  2. Make sure Qualisys is connected
  3. Make sure that the area around the propellers is clear of any obstacles, such as battery cables or tape on the frame. Otherwise Crazyflie will have problems taking off/flying.
  4. Open terminal 1 and run 
    ros2 launch crazyflie launch.py backend:=cflib
    This ROS node works as a server, meaning that it cannot operate the drone independently. It needs to work with the command in terminal 2. Note 1: Make sure everything mentioned before (the Crazyflie's position in the Rviz window, LEDs, logs in the terminal, etc.) looks good before running the second command in terminal 2. Note 2: If you terminate this node and wish to launch it again, make sure to unplug Crazyradio and then plug it back in. The green and yellow LEDs on the Crazyradio indicate a successful connection. Remark 1: If you encounter the following error: 
    “[crazyflie_server-3]   what():  Issue with connection radiobroadcast://*/80/2M. Your radio with firmware 3.2 does not support broadcast communication. Please upgrade your Crazyradio firmware!”
    It can be resolved by commenting out the code block between lines 198 and 203 in crazyflie-link-cpp/src/CrazyradioThread.cpp (as shown here). This is a bug as noted here. Remark 2: Using cflib as backend is important for Crazyradio2.0 as noted here and here.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
1. Make sure the Crazyflie is well balanced, e.g., check if the battery is properly placed.
  2. Before running any ros node, make sure the cfclient is closed.
  3. The Crazyflie battery is charged using the device shown below. Connect the battery to one end of the charger and the micro-USB cable to the other end. Then connect the micro-USB cable to a laptop to supply power for charging.

items.title: Manus Gloves ROS2 Driver
items.text: This is a basic ROS2 driver for Manus Glove. It broadcasts raw skeleton data as ROS2 messages.

items.title: How to Use
items.text:
We tested the driver on Ubuntu 22.04 and ROS2 Humble. It should work with similar environments as well. Here's things you need to do before using it:

  1. Install Manus Core on a Windows machine and upload your license to the dongle. A "Feature" license is required, otherwise you won't get message from Manus SDK.
  2. Clone the repo into a ROS2 workspace, e.g. you should have a folders like this ~/ros2_ws/src/manus_ros2 and ~/ros2_ws/src/manus_ros2_msgs.
  3. Download Manus SDK 2.4.0 and put it under the manus_ros2 folder and rename it as ManusSDK. You should have a folders like this ~/ros2_ws/src/manus_ros2/ManusSDK/include and ~/ros2_ws/src/manus_ros2/ManusSDK/lib.
  4. Follow this guide to install dependencies for Manus SDK. You should follow instructions for the "core Integrated" mode.
  5. Build packages with colcon build and source the environment source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash. Then run ros2 run manus_ros2 rawdata_publisher. Now you should see topics like /manus_node_poses_0 and manus_node_hierarchy_0. There should be a pair of such topics for each glove.

We also include an example client program (in Python) that subscribes to topics of a single glove and controls a Shadow Hand in mujoco in the folder client_scripts. Note that only one glove should be connected. To use this, first source the ROS2 environment. Then install dependencies pip install mujoco open3d mink. We modified the example from mink, a copy of which is already included. When running python manus_data_viz.py, it should open a open3d window and mujoco simulator window. Note that the client program uses inverse kinematics for retargetting. To get better results, you could try setting up a skeleton with Manus SDK directly.

items.title: Loco Positioning System (LPS) configuration
items.text:
Note 1: The instructions provided here for UWB configuration are clear and easy to follow. It is recommended reviewing them carefully to understand each step and how to use the system effectively. The notes below are intended only to highlight a few additional suggestions and differences I encountered. Note 2: The current anchors are already configured and ready to use. If you wish to keep the existing anchor configuration, you only need to complete Step 1 and can then proceed directly to the next section Loco Positioning System usage.

  1. Download and install the Loco Positioning configuration tool (lps-tools) and setup USB access right. Note 1: Installing lps-tools via pip3 requires different dependencies on libraries (pyusb) than installing cfclient. To avoid conflicts in dependencies, create another virtual environment as follows: 
    conda create -n env_2_lpstools python=3.12 # “env_2_lpstools” is the name of this virtual environment and can be changed to other names.
conda activate env_2_lpstools
cd /path/to/lps-tools/respository
pip3 install -e .[pyqt5]
conda deactivate
    Note 2: In step USB access right on Linux here, the sign # should be removed when putting it in the terminal. Check this issue for more details.
  2. Download the Loco Positioning node firmware.
  3. Update the nodes. Note 1: Updating the LPS node through firmware may take several minutes. After clicking the Update button, it turns grey, and it is normal for the progress bar to remain 0% for about a minute before showing any values. Note 2: If you run into the following issue, restarting the computer solves the problem.
  4. Configuring the nodes into anchors.

items.title: Loco Positioning System (LPS) usage
items.text:
1. Connect all anchors to the power source. A complete anchor set should resemble the configuration shown in the following picture. Note 1: The numbers in the top-right corner indicate the anchor IDs. Note 2: When connecting or disconnecting a power bank, always plug and unplug the cable from the power bank end. This approach is easier and helps protect the micro-USB port on the anchor board from wear or damage. Note 3: make sure all powerbanks have enough power the day before conducting experiments.
  2. Turn on the Crazyflie. Note: Communication between the computer and the anchors is relayed through Crazyflie. Therefore, a Crazyflie equipped with an active Loco Positioning Deck must be powered on in order for the anchors to be successfully detected in both cfclient and the ROS 2 driver.
  3. Check anchor status in cfclient. Go to the Loco Positioning tab -> Check the Crazyflie status panel. Anchors that are successfully detected are shown in green boxes, while undetected anchors are shown in red. The reference image below illustrates a successful detection of anchors 0~5, while anchors 6 and 7 are not detected. (Currently, only six anchors are required for localization.) Green dots represent the anchor locations, and the blue dot indicates the estimated tag position. Walk around the space and observe whether the blue dot provides reasonable position estimates.
  4. Place the anchors according to the layout shown in the reference image above. In the current setup, anchors 0~3 are placed on the ground, while anchors 4 and 5 are mounted on the pole. The figure below shows a top-down view of the configuration. All dimensions are given in meters. Note 1: Anchor 0 defines the origin of the coordinate frame. The positions of all other anchors are specified relative to this anchor. Current anchor positions [x,y,z] in meters (they correspond to the coordinates in the step below): 
    an_0: [0.00, 0.00, 0.00]
an_1: [2.70, 0.00, 0.00]
an_2: [2.70, 4.80, 0.00]
an_3: [0.00, 4.80, 0.00]
an_4: [0.00, 2.40, 2.00]
an_5: [2.70, 2.40, 2.00]
    Note 2: The anchor antenna is located at the orange-marked area shown below. Ensure that this point is positioned according to the dimensions specified above. The lab floor mat has dimensions of 0.3 × 0.3 m², which can be used as a convenient reference when arranging the anchors. Note 3: When placing anchors 4 and 5, align the bottom of each anchor stand with the marked line on the pole.
  5. Configure anchor positions (skip this step if the anchor locations do not need to be changed). Click Get from anchors to load the current anchor configuration. When you select and modify a coordinate, it will turn red to indicate an unsaved change. After making the necessary updates, click Write to anchors to save the new configuration. Once the process is complete, all blocks should turn green, as shown in the reference image on the right.
  6. Check measurements using ROS To check out UWB readings of Crazyflie in ROS2, run the following command in the workspace 
    ros2 launch crazyflie launch.py backend:=cflib
    In another terminal, source this workspace and list all available topics using the following command 
    ros2 topic list
    To see the content of each topic, run 
    ros2 topic echo xxx # replace ‘xxx’ with the specific topic name, e.g., /cf2/uwb_data
  7. Record desired topics by opening a new terminal and using 
    ros2 bag record -o bag_name -a
    Note: before launching the command, source the respective workspace to make the topics visible.
  8. Download our code and data from here.
  9. Convert recorded bags to .txt file (convertROSbag2Txt.py) 
    # Usage: 
python3 ./convertROSbag2Txt.py <bag_path> [imu_topic] [uwb_topic] <out_path>
# e.g., 
python3 ./convertROSbag2Txt.py recorded_bag1 /cf2/imu_data /cf2/uwb_data recorded_data_txt
  10. Visualize recorded data (visualizeData.m)
  11. Run a linear least square example (runLinearLS.m)
  12. Run an ESKF example (runESKF.m) Note: You could adjust the initial state, covariance, and measurement noise to see the change in performance. You could also implement the mahalanobis distance in the update step for outline rejection.
  13. Definition of IMU and UWB topics: Note: The topic /cf2/imu_data outputs 6-axis IMU data ["acc.x", "acc.y", "acc.z", "gyro.x", "gyro.y", "gyro.z"], with accelerometer readings of unit \(g\) (9.81 \(m/s^2\)) and gyroscope readings of unit degree/s. The topic /cf2/uwb_data outputs the distance between the tag and the anchor in TWR mode. The following instructions show how to modify them or add UWB measurements from more anchors. Go to the config file crazyswarm2/crazyflie/config/crazyflies.yaml here, under all/firmware_logging/custom_topics, change the vars to what we desire and frequency.
  14. Additional reference: Log IMu data: https://github.com/IMRCLab/crazyswarm2/issues/601 Log UWB data: https://github.com/USC-ACTLab/crazyswarm/issues/283 Others: https://www.bitcraze.io/documentation/repository/lps-node-firmware/master/development/ros/ https://github.com/whoenig/crazyflie_ros/tree/ros2 UWB anchor stand 3D print: https://github.com/bitcraze/bitcraze-mechanics/blob/master/LPS-anchor-stand/anchor-stand.stl

items.title: VINS-Mono Demonstration
items.text: This is instruction of using our handheld demonstrator for VINS-Mono, which is a classical monocular visual SLAM system. The original repository targets ROS1, therefore we use a modified ROS2 version, Qualisys ROS2 project and its ROS messages as the base of our code.

items.title: Equipment Overview
items.text:
The mobile experimental platform is used to record data, then the lab computer is used to run VINS-Mono and evaluate. The mobile experimental platform consists of a Jetson Orin Nano, a RealSense D455 RGB-D camera, and a powerbank. Tracking markers are pre-attached to the platform for use with the camera tracking system.

Safety Instructions:

  • Always verify that the powerbank voltage is set to 12.0V before connecting it to the Jetson Orin Nano.
  • Hold the platform and powerbank securely during data recording.
  • When not in use, place the platform in the designated resting position as shown below to prevent it from tipping over and to keep the markers in their correct positions.

items.title: Environment Setup
items.text:
On the computer: Ensure that all required dependencies are installed on the system (Ubuntu 22.04). 1. Check ROS2 Humble installation. 

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
echo $ROS_DISTRO
If humble is printed, ROS2 Humble is installed correctly. If an error occurs, please install ROS2 Humble by following the official installation guide, then re-run the commands above to verify. 2. Install the system packages required by VINS-Mono. 
sudo apt install libopencv-dev libceres-dev libeigen3-dev
3. Install evo for trajectory evaluation. 
pip install evo
Note: Do not use any Conda virtual environment (Anaconda, Miniconda, etc.), as it is incompatible with ROS. Use the system Python3 installation instead. 4. Install the remaining Python packages required for the evaluation script. 
pip install "numpy<1.25" scipy sophuspy
Then uninstall the pip version of matplotlib to avoid conflicts with the system installation. 
pip uninstall matplotlib

On the Jetson Orin Nano: 1. Install the RealSense ROS2 driver and Qualisys ROS2 driver follow their official guidance. Check the hardware: Connect the RealSense D455 camera to the Jetson Orin Nano via USB-C: 

realsense-viewer  # should be performed directly on the Nano with a monitor
If a viewer window opens displaying color and depth images, the RealSense driver installation is complete. Check the Qualisys driver: 
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
cd mocap_ws
colcon build  # only needed if not previously built
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch qualisys_driver qualisys.launch.py
After launching drivers successfully, open another terminal: 
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
cd mocap_ws
source install/setup.bash
ros2 topic echo /rigid_bodies
If messages are printed to the terminal, the Qualisys driver is functioning correctly.

items.title: Project Workspace Setup
items.text:
On the computer: 1. Create the workspace and install the required repositories. Create the ROS 2 workspace: 

mkdir -p vio/ros2_ws/src && cd vio/ros2_ws/src
Clone the required repositories below into the src directory, then install and configure their dependencies according to each repository’s official documentation.

  • VINS-MONO-ROS2
  • mocap4ros_qualisys
  • mocap4r2_msgs

After setup, add the eval_trajectory.py, trajectory_aligner.py to the vio directory. The final workspace structure should be: 

vio/ 
├── ros2_ws/ 
│   └── src/ 
│       ├── mocap/ 
│       ├── mocap4ros2_qualisys/ 
│       ├── mocap_msgs/ 
│       └── vins_mono_ros2/ 
├── eval_trajectory.py 
└── trajectory_aligner.py
Add the custom configuration file. Place the customized configuration file config_asig.yaml at the following path: 
vio/ros2_ws/src/vins_mono_ros2/config_pkg/config/config_asig.yaml
Make sure the filename and directory structure match exactly, as the system expects the configuration file at this location. 2. Build the ROS Packages. 
cd ros2_ws
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
rm -rf build install log
colcon build
If colcon is not found, install it with: 
sudo apt install python3-colcon-common-extensions

items.title: Ethernet Configuration
items.text: Ensure both the computer and the Jetson Orin Nano are connected to the local Wi-Fi. Open the network settings on the computer and set the IPv4 address of the network interface to Manual. Set the IPv4 address to 192.168.101.xx (for example) where xx can be freely chosen. Set the network mask to 255.255.255.0.

items.title: Launch Drivers on the Jetson Orin Nano
items.text:
From the computer, establish an SSH connection to the Jetson Orin Nano. Note that an SSH connection must be established in every new terminal session before executing commands on the Nano. 1. Launch the RealSense driver. 

# SSH Terminal 1
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run realsense2_camera realsense2_camera_node --ros-args -p unite_imu_method:=2 -p rgb_camera.color_profile:=1280x720x15
2. Launch the Qualisys driver. 
# SSH Terminal 2
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
cd mocap_ws
# colcon build  # only needed if not previously built
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch qualisys_driver qualisys.launch.py
Note: Always verify that the Qualisys driver is publishing correctly before recording the data.

items.title: Record the data
items.text:
Record guidelines

  • Place the platform at the center of the motion capture area before starting.
  • Walk freely within the lab space and ensure the trajectory includes at least one loop closure.
  • Do not approach the edges of the black padding, as this may cause the camera tracking system to lose sight of the markers.
  • Keep the recording duration within approximately 45 seconds, as the Jetson Orin Nano may begin dropping messages beyond this limit.

With both drivers running, begin recording data in a third SSH terminal on Jetson Orin Nano. You may change my_data if desired: 

# SSH Terminal 3
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
# To avoid errors in finding mocap_qualisys topic
cd mocap_ws
source install/setup.bash 
# Record data
mkdir -p ~/example_data  # create directory if it does not exist
ros2 bag record /camera/camera/color/image_raw /camera/camera/imu /rigid_bodies --output example_data/my_data

Once you have completed your recording, press Ctrl+C in SSH Terminal 3 to stop recording. The bag file will be saved to example_data/my_data. Stop both the RealSense and Qualisys drivers at this point.

Transfer the recorded data to the computer.

items.title: Run VINS-Mono
items.text:
On the computer: Run VINS-Mono on your recorded data. In the working directory on the computer, open four terminals and execute the commands in the specified order: 

# Terminal 1
source ros2_ws/install/setup.bash
ros2 launch feature_tracker vins_feature_tracker.launch.py

# Terminal 2
source ros2_ws/install/setup.bash
ros2 launch vins_estimator euroc.launch.py

# Terminal 3
source ros2_ws/install/setup.bash
ros2 bag play example_data/my_data

# Terminal 4
source ros2_ws/install/setup.bash
mkdir -p results/
ros2 bag record --output results/vinsmono_data_my_data /pose_graph/pose_graph_path /vins_estimator/path /rigid_bodies /leica/position
RViz should launch and display the estimated trajectories as below. The orange path represents the estimated trajectory before loop closure, and the green path represents the trajectory after loop closure.

Once the sequence has finished, press Ctrl+C in Terminal 4 to stop recording.

items.title: Evaluation
items.text:
After successfully running VINS-Mono, evaluate the results using the evo package. First, generate the trajectory files: 

python3 eval_trajectory.py --bagpath results/vinsmono_data_my_data --rigid-body-name cam --save-path ./results/
This script displays a plot of the ground truth and estimated trajectories, and saves them as: 
results/gt_traj.txt
results/est_traj.txt
Then run the evaluation: 
evo_ape tum results/gt_traj.txt results/est_traj.txt --align --plot
This computes the Absolute Pose Error (APE) of the estimated trajectory. A mean translation error of approximately 0.1 - 0.2m is expected.
